basic_identification.name: Physical-digital hybrid installations
basic_identification.originator: teamLab (founded 2001, Tokyo), Random International (founded 2005, London), Studio Drift / DRIFT (Lonneke Gordijn & Ralph Nauta, Amsterdam), Meow Wolf (Santa Fe), Refik Anadol, Moment Factory. Broader lineage from Nam June Paik, Bill Viola, Olafur Eliasson
basic_identification.geography: Global. Major permanent venues: Tokyo (teamLab Borderless, teamLab Planets), Abu Dhabi (teamLab Phenomena, opening 2025), Jeddah, Hamburg (UBS Digital Art Museum, opening 2026), Amsterdam (DRIFT Museum, 2025), Santa Fe/Las Vegas/Houston/Denver (Meow Wolf)

core_ideas.core_claim: Digital art achieves its full potential when it envelops the body in physical space, creating immersive environments where visitors become participants. Technology should merge with natural and architectural elements to produce experiences that transcend screen-based engagement. teamLab's philosophy: 'technology is not in conflict with nature.'
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Entirely dependent on digital technology: projection mapping (38.9% of 2024 immersive market revenue), real-time rendering, sensors, computer vision, interactive software, LED arrays, spatial audio. The digital specificity lies in the responsiveness — environments that react to presence, movement, and collective behavior in ways impossible with static physical media.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Complex and contradictory. These installations are attention economy powerhouses: teamLab's business model depends on social media sharing — user-generated content accounts for roughly half of annual ticket sales, cutting customer acquisition costs 30-40%. The practice optimizes for 'Instagrammable moments.' Yet the physical, embodied experience is irreducible to screen capture. The tension between the shareability that drives revenue and the somatic immersion that defines the art is the practice's central paradox.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Mixed. The declared intention is to create transformative experiences of beauty, nature, and interconnection. The economic reality is attention capture through spectacle. Some practitioners (Studio Drift, Random International) emphasize conceptual depth and critical engagement. Others (Immersive Van Gogh, Monet's Garden) are pure commercial spectacle with no artistic intention beyond entertainment. The practice spans the full spectrum from intention to attention.

market_economics.revenue_model: Ticket sales (62.45% of 2024 immersive entertainment revenue), sponsorship (UBS for Hamburg museum), merchandise, hospitality, licensing, corporate commissions. teamLab Planets generates approximately $60 million annual revenue from 2.5 million visitors at ~$25/ticket. Subscription and membership models growing (projected 24.76% CAGR). Some installations commission from galleries at $100,000-$1,000,000+.
market_economics.market_position: Primary experience market (ticket sales), with secondary gallery market for smaller works by the same artists. Infrastructure position through dedicated venues (permanent museums). teamLab operates as both artist collective and entertainment company.
market_economics.price_range: Tickets: $20-$45 per person. Gallery works by Refik Anadol: $50,000-$5,000,000+. Studio Drift gallery works via Pace Gallery: $100,000+. The practice spans mass-market entertainment pricing and high-end art market pricing.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Strong growth. Immersive entertainment market projected to reach $412.69 billion by 2030 (CAGR 23.41%). teamLab expanding globally (Abu Dhabi, Hamburg, Jeddah). DRIFT opening dedicated museum in Amsterdam 2025. Meow Wolf expanding to multiple cities. However, the market may face saturation as the novelty effect diminishes.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Two distinct audiences. Mass-market visitors: families, tourists, social media users, experience seekers (2.5 million at teamLab Planets alone). Art collectors: high-net-worth individuals and institutions buying gallery works by Anadol, DRIFT, Random International. Institutional buyers acquiring for permanent collections. The mass market is the revenue driver; the collector market provides art-world legitimacy. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: High commercial sustainability for established operators (teamLab, Meow Wolf). The entertainment model generates recurring revenue independent of speculative interest. However, sustainability questions arise around: technology maintenance costs, novelty fatigue (will visitors return?), energy consumption of projection systems, and whether the format can evolve beyond its current formula. Critical sustainability is more questionable — can the practice maintain artistic depth under commercial pressure?

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Projection mapping systems, TouchDesigner, Unity, Unreal Engine, custom software (teamLab uses proprietary systems), LED arrays, kinetic sculpture mechanisms, spatial audio systems, computer vision (depth cameras, lidar), water/fog/mirror systems for physical effects, architectural design. High-end hardware: Christie/Barco projectors, custom sensors, industrial robotics (for kinetic works).
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Increasingly integrated. Refik Anadol is the most prominent AI-immersive artist, using machine learning to generate large-scale data visualizations. teamLab's systems use algorithmic rules but not ML in most works. DRIFT uses computational models of natural behavior (flocking algorithms). AI threatens the practice by potentially automating content generation, but the physical infrastructure remains irreplaceable. The frontier is AI-responsive environments that learn from visitor behavior.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Real-time and interactive. Environments respond to visitor presence, movement, touch, and collective behavior. teamLab's works change based on audience actions. Random International's Rain Room pauses rain where bodies are detected. DRIFT's kinetic works move autonomously. The liveness is embodied and spatial, not screen-based.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Partially developed. Terms include: immersive, interactive, responsive, experiential, embodied, multi-sensory, spatial computing, projection mapping, digital nature. The Art Newspaper's Ben Luke described it as a 'hybrid format between installation and son et lumieres.' The vocabulary struggles to distinguish between critical installation art and commercial spectacle. Art criticism often defaults to spectacle/anti-spectacle binaries rather than developing nuanced analytical tools for evaluating immersive experience.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Tends toward enclosure (proprietary technology, ticketed venues), capture (social media optimization), spectacle (prioritizing visual impact over critical depth), and both individual and collective (solo experiences within collective environments). The practice sits on the spectacle end of the spectacle-infrastructure axis, the enclosure end of the openness-enclosure axis, but the commons end of the individual-collective axis (shared experience).

infrastructure_governance.openness: Largely proprietary. teamLab's software is proprietary and closely guarded. Studio technologies are trade secrets. Financial details are not disclosed (teamLab remains private with limited financial disclosures). Some artists (Refik Anadol) share conceptual frameworks but not technical implementations. The open-source community around TouchDesigner is adjacent but distinct from the major studios.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Corporate/studio. teamLab operates as a company with 600+ members. DRIFT is an artist studio with gallery representation (Pace). Random International is a studio with project-based work. Meow Wolf is a for-profit company. No community governance, DAO, or democratic decision-making. Artistic direction controlled by founders/creative directors.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Visitors have no data sovereignty. Venues collect presence data through sensors and cameras. Social media sharing generates data for platforms. Artists' proprietary systems are not transparent about data collection or use. No opt-out mechanisms for in-venue sensing. This is a significant blind spot in the practice.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low. Each installation is a bespoke, self-contained system. No standardized formats or protocols. Works cannot be easily transferred between venues or platforms. Each new installation requires custom development. The lack of interoperability is both a creative choice (each work is unique) and a business strategy (preventing easy replication).
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Challenging. Installations depend on specific hardware configurations, real-time software, and spatial contexts that resist preservation. teamLab's permanent venues serve as living archives. Documentation through video captures fragments but not the embodied experience. Museum acquisitions face significant conservation challenges. The practice is inherently at-risk from technological obsolescence.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Minimal. Ticket purchase implies consent to be in a sensored environment. No granular consent for data collection, photography, or behavioral tracking within venues. Terms of service cover legal requirements but not meaningful consent. The practice lags significantly behind best practice in consent architecture.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Complex absorption. Major museums now host immersive exhibitions (V&A, High Museum, Amos Rex). Gallery representation for key artists (DRIFT at Pace, Anadol at various galleries). But the art establishment maintains skepticism: critics dismiss the format as entertainment, not art. The tension between mass appeal and critical legitimacy defines the practice's institutional position. The UBS Digital Art Museum in Hamburg represents a new institutional form — purpose-built for immersive digital art.
field_position.what_it_enables: Mass engagement with digital art beyond screen-based viewing. Bodily, embodied experience of computational systems. Revenue models that sustain large-scale digital art production. A bridge between entertainment and art that brings millions into contact with technology-driven creative work. Global touring and permanent venue models for digital art.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Critical depth commensurate with its scale. Transparency about technology and business models. Open infrastructure that could benefit the broader field. Meaningful consent architecture for visitor data. Preservation strategies for born-digital installations. A critical vocabulary adequate to evaluate the form on its own terms rather than through the spectacle/anti-spectacle binary. Diversity of voices — the major practitioners are predominantly from wealthy nations.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Economically: ticket prices ($20-45) exclude lower-income audiences, despite being cheaper than most concert tickets. Geographically: permanent venues are in wealthy global cities. Physically: many installations have limited accessibility for disabled visitors (teamLab Planets requires barefoot wading). Creatively: the proprietary technology and high production costs exclude independent artists. Critically: the entertainment framing excludes those seeking critical engagement. [uncertain]
field_position.frontier_signal: Established and expanding. The format is the dominant exhibition model for digital art in 2024-2025. Growth continues through new venues and global expansion. The frontier is in AI-responsive environments, mixed reality integration, and the development of dedicated institutional infrastructure (UBS Hamburg, DRIFT Amsterdam). The question is whether the format evolves or becomes formulaic.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Social media (Instagram, TikTok — user-generated content is primary discovery channel), tourism platforms (TripAdvisor, Google), word of mouth, traditional advertising, press coverage, art publications. Algorithm-driven discovery is central — teamLab's model depends on viral social media sharing.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Very high. The business model is built on attention: social media sharing drives 50% of ticket sales. Without Instagram/TikTok, customer acquisition costs would roughly double. The practice would survive platform disappearance (the physical experience has inherent value) but the revenue model would require fundamental restructuring.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Primarily attention-native in its business model. The intention to create transformative experiences is genuine but subordinated to the attention mechanics that sustain the operation. Some practitioners (Studio Drift, Random International) are more intention-aligned through gallery and institutional work. The mass-market immersive model is structurally attention-dependent.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Low. Proprietary technology, closed business models, no open-source contributions. The practice generates shared cultural experience (millions of visitors) but does not contribute to shared technical infrastructure, open tools, or public knowledge. The commons contribution is experiential, not structural.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Ownership provenance for gallery works (standard art market tracking). No provenance tracking for the immersive experience itself. Visitor experiences are ephemeral and untracked beyond anonymized data. The practice does not engage with meaning provenance or the evolution of interpretation over time.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Real-time (interactive responses), cyclical (seasonal/tidal changes in some teamLab works), but fundamentally present-tense. The experience is designed for the now — not archival, not anticipatory. Some works reference natural cycles (DRIFT's plant-based kinetics, teamLab's seasons) but the temporal logic is predominantly immediate and experiential.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The practice is focused on presence — filling space with sensation. It does not systematically address what is absent from the field. If anything, the overwhelming presence of spectacle obscures what is missing: critical depth, open infrastructure, consent architecture, preservation strategies. The practice is about maximal presence, not absence detection.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Consensus within studios (artistic direction controlled by founders) rather than coherence across the field. The broader immersive art field lacks coherence — it encompasses critical installation art, commercial entertainment, and everything in between with no shared framework for evaluation. The spectacle/anti-spectacle debate prevents productive dialogue.
coherence.contestability: Low within studios (founder-directed). High in the critical discourse (heated debates about whether immersive art is real art). Critics like Ben Luke can challenge the format, and practitioners respond. But visitors (the primary audience) have no formal mechanism to contest or shape the work. The contestation happens between critics and producers, not between audiences and creators.
coherence.forkability: Low. The practice requires massive capital investment ($10M+ for a permanent venue), proprietary technology, and specialized teams. Individual artists cannot fork teamLab's model. However, the conceptual approach (immersive, interactive, sensor-driven) is infinitely forkable at smaller scales. TouchDesigner workshops enable independent practitioners to create small-scale interactive installations.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The proof that digital art can engage mass audiences through embodied experience. The understanding that physical presence and digital computation can be integrated without subordinating one to the other. The demonstration that digital art can generate sustainable revenue through experience rather than object sales. DRIFT's research into natural systems as computational models.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The attention-capture business model that subordinates artistic depth to social media optimization. The proprietary technology enclosure that prevents knowledge sharing. The absence of consent architecture for visitor data. The spectacle-first approach that treats critical engagement as optional. The opacity of financial and technological operations. The individual-genius studio model that concentrates creative authority.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Physical-digital hybrid installations prove that digital art can be spatially embodied and commercially sustainable — but through enclosure and spectacle. A(DAI) seeks openness and infrastructure. The tension is between proven commercial viability (the installations) and the commons-first model (A(DAI)). Can A(DAI) achieve the embodied engagement without the enclosure? Can infrastructure be as compelling as spectacle?

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Moderate. Venues face standard entertainment/venue regulations (safety, accessibility, fire codes). Data collection through sensors may face GDPR/privacy regulations in the EU. Energy consumption may face environmental regulations. AI-generated content in installations may trigger EU AI Act disclosure requirements. No specific art-regulatory exposure. Copyright is straightforward — works are original creations.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: All rights reserved. Studios protect proprietary technology and artistic designs through trade secrets, patents, and copyright. Gallery works sold with standard art market rights (reproduction rights retained or licensed). No open-source or Creative Commons elements. The IP model is maximally enclosed.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Implicit opt-in through ticket purchase. No granular consent for specific data collection within venues. Privacy policies exist but are standard-issue, not designed for meaningful consent. The practice does not engage with the opt-in/opt-out question as a design consideration.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Moderate. Social media platforms (Instagram, TikTok) are critical for marketing but not for the art itself. Physical venues are independently operated. Technology suppliers (projector manufacturers, sensor companies) are replaceable. The main dependency is on the physical venue infrastructure and the proprietary software stack. No blockchain or single-platform dependency.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong positive network effects. More venues create more social media content, driving more awareness and more visitors. teamLab's global expansion creates a network of interconnected experiences. The brand recognition compounds. However, network effects also create competition fatigue — too many immersive experiences may dilute the market.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Unaffected by the 2022-2023 crypto/NFT crash. The practice operates on ticket sales and institutional commissions, not speculative markets. Growth has been continuous: teamLab Planets expanded in January 2025, teamLab Phenomena opening in Abu Dhabi April 2025, UBS Hamburg opening 2026, DRIFT museum Amsterdam 2025. The trajectory is strong expansion, though market saturation is a long-term risk.
